Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) is a cooperative surveillance technology that has become a key component of modern air-traffic management. Suitably equipped aircraft periodically broadcast their International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) 24-bit address, callsign, position, altitude, ground speed, heading and vertical rate. This project, "Design and Implementation of a Real-Time Aircraft Tracking and Trajectory Prediction System", presents an end-to-end platform that receives the structured binary stream supplied by a uAvionix PingStation, separates it into complete frames, decodes and normalises aircraft records, stores continuous per-aircraft trajectory histories, predicts short communication gaps using sliding-window linear regression with a deterministic kinematic fallback, and presents the live air picture through a Flask and Leaflet.js browser interface.

The work spans both electronics/communication and computer-science aspects. The report examines the 1090 MHz Mode-S Extended-Squitter physical layer, including Pulse-Position Modulation, the preamble, frame structure and radio-propagation considerations, while recognising that the PingStation performs RF demodulation and exposes a higher-level length-prefixed stream to the software. The implemented software is divided into acquisition, decoding, preprocessing, storage/prediction and presentation layers. Live hardware and recorded simulation data pass through the same decoder, while session-specific HEX, ASCII, exact-stream and intermediate decoded logs support repeatable testing and diagnosis.

The system has been exercised with both live PingStation reception and replay of recorded PingStation data. Functional testing verified dynamic ICAO detection, continuous SQLite and per-aircraft Excel logging, automatic creation of a master workbook, one-second dashboard updates, live/simulation switching, short-outage trajectory prediction and resumption of actual tracking when reception returns. Prediction is deliberately limited to a configurable short horizon (180 seconds by default), because extrapolation uncertainty grows rapidly during turns and speed changes. The current predictor is an interpretable machine-learning baseline rather than a trained deep-neural model; Kalman filtering and recurrent sequence models remain appropriate subjects for future comparative research.

the continual process of determining the identity, position and intent of aircraft operating within a given volume of airspace

is one of the central pillars of safe and efficient aviation. For more than half a century this function was performed almost exclusively by ground-based radar: Primary Surveillance Radar (PSR), which detects the echo of a transmitted pulse reflected from an aircraft's airframe, and Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR), which interrogates an on-board transponder and receives a coded reply containing identity and altitude information (Mode A/C, and later Mode S). While radar-based surveillance has served aviation well, it suffers from well-known limitations: it is expensive to install and maintain, its update rate is constrained by antenna rotation speed (typically 4Ã¢â‚¬â€œ12 seconds per scan), its accuracy degrades with range due to beam spreading, and it provides only an external, ground-derived estimate of an aircraft's state rather than the aircraft's own, more precise, satellite-derived measurements.

Automatic Dependent SurveillanceÃ¢â‚¬â€œBroadcast (ADS-B) was conceived as a technology that would overcome these limitations by inverting the surveillance paradigm: instead of a ground station interrogating an aircraft, the aircraft itself periodically broadcasts Ã¢â‚¬â€ typically once or twice per second Ã¢â‚¬â€ a self-generated report of its own state vector, derived primarily from an on-board Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver and other avionics sensors. The term is best understood by decomposing it: the surveillance is Automatic because it requires no pilot or controller action; it is Dependent because the quality of the reported position depends on the aircraft's own navigation sources; and it is Broadcast because the report is transmitted omnidirectionally to any suitably equipped receiver Ã¢â‚¬â€ whether mounted in another aircraft (for Airborne Collision Avoidance and self-separation), at an Air Navigation Service Provider's ground station, or, as is increasingly the case, in the hands of hobbyists, researchers and students operating low-cost Software-Defined Radio (SDR) receivers.

In the international civil aviation context, ADS-B is mandated by regulators such as the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), under its NextGen modernisation programme, and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), and is standardised by the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) and by RTCA documents such as DO-260B. Two principal data links are used worldwide: the 1090 MHz Extended Squitter (1090ES), which re-uses the existing Mode-S transponder infrastructure and is the dominant link for air-transport category aircraft, and the 978 MHz Universal Access Transceiver (UAT) link used mainly by general-aviation aircraft in United States airspace below eighteen-thousand feet. This project concentrates on the 1090 MHz Extended Squitter link because of its global ubiquity and because low-cost receiver hardware for this band is widely available
a decisive practical consideration for an academic, laboratory-scale implementation.
The growing availability of inexpensive RTL-SDR dongles and purpose-built receiver front-ends

such as the uAvionix PingStation device used in this project Ã¢â‚¬â€ together with mature open-source decoding libraries, has placed what was once specialised aerospace instrumentation within reach of undergraduate laboratories. This presents a unique opportunity: a student project can, with a modest budget, capture *real* broadcast signals from aircraft passing overhead, decode them down to the bit level, and build a complete, end-to-end surveillance and analysis pipeline that mirrors Ã¢â‚¬â€ in miniature Ã¢â‚¬â€ the architecture of operational air-traffic-management systems. It is precisely this opportunity that motivated the present work.

Three considerations motivated the choice of this project topic. First, ADS-B sits at the intersection of electronics and communication engineering and computer science: understanding it requires familiarity with radio-frequency propagation, modulation and coding theory, digital-signal processing and antenna design on the one hand, and with software architecture, databases, web technologies and data visualisation on the other. A project built around ADS-B therefore offers an unusually rich platform for demonstrating the integration of theory from across the Electronics & Communication Engineering curriculum Ã¢â‚¬â€ RF and microwave engineering, digital communication, antenna theory, embedded systems, and computer networks Ã¢â‚¬â€ within a single, coherent system.

Second, live aircraft-tracking systems possess an immediate, tangible appeal: the data is real, it is continuously generated by aircraft that can often be seen or heard overhead, and the resulting visualisation Ã¢â‚¬â€ a moving map populated with aircraft icons, callsigns, altitudes and projected tracks Ã¢â‚¬â€ provides instant, intuitive feedback on whether the underlying decoding and processing pipeline is functioning correctly. This makes the system both an effective demonstration of engineering competence and a genuinely useful tool that can be operated long after the academic submission deadline has passed.

Third, by building the system from first principles Ã¢â‚¬â€ writing the decoder logic, the database schema, the trajectory-prediction mathematics and the web dashboard rather than simply deploying an existing turnkey package Ã¢â‚¬â€ the project offers maximal opportunity for learning. Each subsystem (RF front-end characterisation, frame decoding, data validation, persistent storage, predictive analytics and interactive visualisation) exercises a distinct skill set, and the integration of these subsystems into a single coherent application demonstrates systems-engineering competence that a narrower, single-topic project would not.
The project was undertaken with the following specific objectives:

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ To study the physical-layer characteristics of the 1090 MHz Mode-S Extended Squitter (ADS-B) signal Ã¢â‚¬â€ its modulation scheme, preamble structure, frame format and error-detection mechanism Ã¢â‚¬â€ and to relate these characteristics to the design requirements of a practical receiving system.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ To set up and characterise a low-cost RF front-end (uAvionix PingStation receiver with a 1090 MHz co-linear/discone antenna) capable of capturing live ADS-B broadcasts from aircraft within line-of-sight range of the laboratory.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ To design and implement a software pipeline that ingests the raw hexadecimal Mode-S message log produced by the receiver, decodes and validates Downlink-Format-17 (DF17) Extended Squitter frames, and extracts state-vector parameters (identity, position, altitude, velocity and heading).

â€¢ To design a compact FlightTrajectoryStore that maintains the latest state and timestamped trajectory samples in SQLite, while automatically creating session-based per-ICAO Excel files, a master workbook, and diagnostic HEX, ASCII, raw and exact-stream logs.

â€¢ To develop an interpretable short-outage trajectory predictor based on sliding-window linear regression over recent real observations, with a constant-velocity kinematic fallback and a configurable maximum prediction age.

â€¢ To build an interactive browser dashboard using Flask, Leaflet.js and Chart.js, including smooth aircraft movement, actual and predicted track overlays, aircraft/route information, a resizable detail panel, live status feedback, and a direct simulation-mode switch.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ To evaluate the resulting system experimentally: to characterise its message-decoding accuracy, geographic reception range, trajectory-prediction error, end-to-end latency and update rate, and to compare these figures against the published characteristics of comparable open-source and commercial ADS-B tracking platforms.

The scope of the present work is deliberately bounded to a single PingStation receiver and the structured stream emitted by that receiver. The software does not demodulate raw I/Q samples; instead, it receives length-prefixed PingStation frames over TCP or replays captured frames through the same decoder. Multilateration and independent verification of an aircraft's self-reported position are outside the current implementation. The trajectory predictor uses recent observations from the current session and is intended to bridge short reception gaps, not to reconstruct complete flight plans or make long-horizon strategic forecasts. Advanced filters and trained sequence models are therefore treated as future comparative extensions.

On the software side, the system is implemented as a single-process Flask application intended for deployment on a single host machine (a laboratory PC or a small single-board computer); horizontal scaling, multi-tenant deployment and production-grade security hardening are not within scope, although the architecture has been designed so that such extensions would not require a fundamental redesign. The user interface targets modern desktop and mobile web browsers; native mobile applications are not provided.

The remainder of this report is organised into four further chapters, followed by the references, bibliography and appendix. Chapter 2 reviews the literature relevant to the project: it traces the historical evolution of aircraft surveillance technology from primary radar through Mode-S Secondary Surveillance Radar to ADS-B, surveys the international regulatory and standardisation landscape, examines existing open-source and commercial ADS-B decoding and tracking platforms, and reviews published approaches to flight-trajectory prediction. Chapter 3 forms the technical core of the report: it documents the methodology and the work carried out, beginning with the requirements analysis and system overview, proceeding through a detailed treatment of the radio-frequency front-end and the Mode-S Extended-Squitter physical and link layers, and concluding with a complete description of the software architecture, the data-acquisition and decoding pipeline, the database design, the trajectory-prediction algorithm, the aircraft-classification logic and the user-interface design. Chapter 4 presents the experimental results obtained from operating the system with live and simulated traffic, characterises its performance along several axes, and compares it against published figures for comparable systems. Chapter 5 summarises the work, draws conclusions, candidly discusses the limitations of the implementation, and proposes a roadmap for future enhancement. The report closes with a list of references in IEEE citation format, a bibliography of further reading consulted during the project, and an appendix containing supplementary material such as sample raw
message logs, code excerpts and a consolidated glossary of ADS-B-related terminology.

The history of aircraft surveillance is, in large part, the history of radar. Primary Surveillance Radar (PSR), developed during the Second World War, determines an aircraft's range and bearing by measuring the time-of-flight and angle-of-arrival of a reflected microwave pulse; it requires no cooperation from the aircraft and can therefore detect non-cooperative or non-transponder-equipped targets, but it cannot directly determine an aircraft's identity or altitude, and its performance is strongly affected by the target's radar cross-section, by weather (ground clutter, precipitation) and by terrain masking. Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR), introduced in the 1950s, addressed the identity problem by having the ground station transmit a coded interrogation pulse train that triggers an on-board transponder to reply with an encoded identity (Mode A) and, later, pressure altitude (Mode C). Mode S Ã¢â‚¬â€ standardised by ICAO in the 1980s Ã¢â‚¬â€ extended this scheme with selective addressing (each aircraft is assigned a unique 24-bit ICAO address), reducing the "garbling" that occurred when multiple aircraft replied simultaneously, and introduced a general-purpose data-link capability that could carry richer information than the simple identity/altitude codes of Modes A and C [1], [2].

It is this Mode-S data-link capability that ADS-B exploits. Rather than waiting to be interrogated, a Mode-S transponder configured for Extended-Squitter operation periodically and spontaneously transmits Ã¢â‚¬â€ "squitters" Ã¢â‚¬â€ a 112-bit message (Downlink Format 17) containing, among other things, the aircraft's GNSS-derived position (encoded using the Compact Position Reporting, or CPR, scheme), barometric or geometric altitude, velocity vector, and identification/category information [3]. Because this information originates on board the aircraft and is derived from satellite navigation rather than from a ground-based measurement, its accuracy is frequently superior to that obtainable from radar Ã¢â‚¬â€ a major factor behind the international decision to mandate ADS-B Out equipage on commercial and, increasingly, general-aviation aircraft [4], [5].
2.2 ADS-B Standards and the Regulatory Landscape

The technical specification of the 1090 MHz Extended-Squitter ADS-B link is documented in RTCA DO-260 and its subsequent revisions DO-260A and DO-260B, which define the message formats, encoding rules, and the Minimum Operational Performance Standards (MOPS) that avionics equipment must satisfy [6]. ICAO Annex 10, Volume IV, provides the international Standards and Recommended Practices (SARPs) for Mode-S and ADS-B, ensuring that equipment built to different national specifications remains globally interoperable [2]. On the regulatory side, the United States Federal Aviation Administration's ADS-B Out mandate (effective 1 January 2020) requires aircraft operating in defined categories of airspace to broadcast ADS-B Out messages compliant with DO-260B, as part of the wider NextGen air-traffic-modernisation programme [7]. The European Union, through EASA and the Single European Sky ATM Research (SESAR) programme, has issued analogous requirements for ADS-B-equipage in European airspace [8]. These mandates have ensured that an overwhelming majority of commercial air transport aircraft, and a rapidly growing fraction of general-aviation aircraft, now broadcast ADS-B continuously Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is precisely what makes a student-built ADS-B receiver project both feasible and rewarding: there is, quite literally, always live data to receive.

It is worth noting, for completeness, that a second ADS-B data link exists: the 978 MHz Universal Access Transceiver (UAT) link, used predominantly by general-aviation aircraft operating below eighteen-thousand feet within United States airspace, as an alternative to the 1090ES link for aircraft that do not already carry a Mode-S transponder [9]. Because 1090 MHz Extended-Squitter is the link used worldwide by air-transport category aircraft, and because suitable receiver hardware for this band is comparatively easy to obtain, this project restricts its scope to the 1090ES link, as discussed in Section 1.4.
2.3 Existing Open-Source and Commercial ADS-B Platforms

A vibrant open-source ecosystem has grown up around ADS-B reception, driven largely by the wide availability of inexpensive RTL2832U-based USB software-defined-radio dongles. Foremost among the open-source decoders is dump1090,

originally written by Salvatore Sanfilippo and subsequently forked and extended by numerous contributors (notably the FlightAware and readsb variants), which demodulates the raw I/Q samples from an RTL-SDR device, detects Mode-S preambles, decodes DF17/DF18 Extended-Squitter frames, and exposes the resulting aircraft table through both a textual interface and a built-in web map [10]. Crowd-sourced aggregation networks such as FlightAware, ADS-B Exchange and the academically-oriented OpenSky Network collect feeds from thousands of volunteer-operated ground stations worldwide and republish the combined picture Ã¢â‚¬â€ OpenSky, in particular, also makes large historical datasets available for research purposes and has published extensively on data-quality and coverage characteristics of crowd-sourced ADS-B networks [11], [12]. Commercial platforms such as FlightRadar24 and PlaneFinder provide polished, consumer-facing visualisations built on similar underlying decoding pipelines, often supplemented with proprietary radar and schedule data to fill coverage gaps [13].

The Python ecosystem additionally provides decoding libraries such as pyModeS, which implements the bit-level decoding rules for the various Downlink Formats and Extended-Squitter sub-types in a well-documented, research-friendly form, and has been used as a reference for verifying the correctness of the decoding logic implemented in the present project [14]. Hardware vendors such as uAvionix have, more recently, brought to market purpose-built receiver appliances Ã¢â‚¬â€ including the PingStation device used as the RF front-end for this project Ã¢â‚¬â€ that perform the demodulation and framing in dedicated firmware and expose the decoded messages as a structured hexadecimal log stream over a simple interface, considerably simplifying the acquisition stage of a project such as this one [15]. The present work draws on the architectural lessons of dump1090 and pyModeS while adopting the PingStation as an acquisition front-end, and builds, on top of that foundation, an original storage, prediction and visualisation layer tailored to the project's objectives.

Predicting an aircraft's future position from its currently observed state is a long-standing problem in air-traffic management, with applications ranging from short-term conflict detection to strategic flow management. The simplest class of techniques sometimes called "dead-reckoning" or "linear extrapolation" methods projects the

aircraft's position forward in time by assuming that its current ground speed and heading remain constant; on the spherical Earth, this projection is most correctly performed along a great-circle path using standard geodesic forward-projection formulas (the "direct geodesic problem") [16]. Such methods are computationally inexpensive and require no information beyond the most recent state vector, but their accuracy degrades over longer horizons because real flights are rarely perfectly straight: aircraft climb, descend, change heading to follow airway structure, and are vectored by air-traffic control.

More sophisticated approaches incorporate additional information to improve accuracy over longer horizons. Flight-plan-based methods use the aircraft's filed route and published airway/waypoint structure to constrain the predicted path; trajectory-clustering and case-based-reasoning methods match the observed initial segment of a flight against a database of historically observed trajectories between the same originÃ¢â‚¬â€œdestination pair; and, most recently, machine-learning approaches Ã¢â‚¬â€ including recurrent neural networks, sequence-to-sequence models and Gaussian-process regression Ã¢â‚¬â€ have been applied to learn manoeuvre patterns directly from large historical trajectory datasets such as those published by the OpenSky Network [17], [18]. These data-driven methods can achieve markedly better accuracy over horizons of tens of minutes, but they require substantial training data, computational resources for model training, and careful validation Ã¢â‚¬â€ requirements that lie beyond the scope of an undergraduate project of this size and duration.

Given these considerations, the present project adopts sliding-window ordinary least-squares linear regression as its primary short-outage predictor. Separate functions of time are fitted to the most recent latitude, longitude and altitude samples for each aircraft, reducing the influence of any single noisy observation compared with two-point extrapolation. When too few valid samples are available, the system falls back to constant-velocity kinematics based on the most recent speed, heading and vertical rate. This combination is computationally light, explainable during evaluation, independent of a large pre-trained dataset, and suitable for the project's real-time single-host environment.
2.5 Summary and Identification of the Research Gap

The literature surveyed above shows that, while both the underlying ADS-B technology and a number of mature open-source decoding tools are well documented, there are comparatively few published, complete, end-to-end *educational* reference implementations that integrate Ã¢â‚¬â€ within a single, coherently engineered codebase Ã¢â‚¬â€ RF-front-end acquisition, Extended-Squitter decoding, persistent storage, trajectory prediction and an interactive visual dashboard, while also documenting, at an undergraduate level of detail, the relevant electronics-and-communication theory that underpins each stage. Existing tools such as dump1090 and pyModeS are excellent at the decoding stage but provide little in the way of persistent storage, predictive analytics or polished visualisation; commercial platforms provide polished visualisation but are closed-source and document neither their internal architecture nor the underlying RF theory. This project addresses that gap by building, end to end, a complete and openly documented system the work described in the chapters that follow that can additionally serve as a teaching and demonstration platform for future students of Electronics & Communication Engineering.

The system developed in this project, referred to throughout this report as the ADS-B Aircraft Tracker, is an end-to-end pipeline that begins at the antenna terminal and ends at the user's web browser. Figure 1.1 illustrates, at a conceptual level, the overall idea: an aircraft equipped with a Mode-S Extended-Squitter transponder periodically broadcasts its state vector on 1090 MHz; this broadcast is received by a ground station within line-of-sight range; the ground station decodes the broadcast and forwards the resulting structured data to a processing and storage stage; and the processed data is finally rendered, in real time, on an interactive map displayed to the end user.

Before any design decisions were made, a short requirements-analysis exercise was carried out to establish the functional and non-functional requirements that the system would need to satisfy. The functional requirements identified were: (i) the system must be able to acquire live Mode-S Extended-Squitter broadcasts using the laboratory's PingStation receiver, as well as to operate, for development and

demonstration purposes, on pre-recorded or simulated traffic when no live receiver is available; (ii) it must decode DF17/DF18 frames into structured records containing identity, position, altitude, speed, heading and vertical-rate information; (iii) it must persist these records, together with a continuously updated trajectory history for each aircraft, in a queryable form; (iv) it must compute and display a short-term predicted track for each aircraft; and (v) it must present the resulting information through an interactive, near-real-time web interface, including a map view, search/selection functionality, and an information panel showing identity, type, photograph and current state for the selected aircraft.
The non-functional requirements identified were: the system should sustain an update ("refresh") rate of at least 1 Hz so that the displayed picture appears smooth and current; end-to-end latency

from message reception to display update should remain low enough (sub-second to a few seconds) that the displayed picture does not feel stale; the system should run on a single, modest laboratory PC without requiring specialised server infrastructure; and it should degrade gracefully for instance, by falling back to a simulated feed when the RF front-end is temporarily unavailable, so that development, testing and demonstration are not blocked by hardware availability. 3.2 The 1090 MHz Mode-S Extended-Squitter Physical Layer

Because this is a project in Electronics & Communication Engineering, particular care was taken to understand Ã¢â‚¬â€ not merely to use Ã¢â‚¬â€ the physical-layer characteristics of the signal being received. This section documents that understanding, since it directly informed several implementation decisions (for example, the message-validation logic described in Section 3.4 relies on knowledge of the exact frame structure and the cyclic-redundancy-check convention described below).

The Extended-Squitter downlink operates on a single, internationally allocated carrier frequency of 1090 MHz, within the L-band of the radio spectrum. This frequency was originally chosen for Mode-S because it coincides with the reply frequency already used by legacy Mode A/C transponders, allowing Mode-S equipment to be backward compatible with the existing secondary-radar infrastructure. At this frequency, propagation is essentially line-of-sight: the signal does not diffract significantly around the curvature of the Earth or around large obstructions such as hills, and the maximum theoretical reception range is therefore governed by the radio-horizon distance, which depends on the height of both the transmitting (airborne) and receiving (ground-station) antennas above the local terrain. For a ground station at height h_r (in metres) and an aircraft at height h_t, the combined radio-horizon distance, in kilometres, may be approximated by the well-known relation d Ã¢â€°Ë† 3.57 (Ã¢Ë†Å¡h_r + Ã¢Ë†Å¡h_t); for a typical laboratory rooftop installation at roughly 20 m above the surrounding terrain, and a cruising aircraft at 10,000 m, this evaluates to a theoretical maximum range of approximately 16 + 357 Ã¢â€°Ë† 373 km, a figure broadly consistent with the reception ranges reported in Chapter 4.

In practice, the achievable range is also a function of the transmitted power (Mode-S transponders typically radiate between 125 W and 500 W peak pulse power, depending on equipment class), the receiving antenna's gain and radiation pattern, feeder-cable losses, and the receiver's noise figure and sensitivity. The PingStation receiver front-end used in this project specifies a sensitivity of approximately Ã¢Ë†â€™84 dBm for reliable Extended-Squitter decoding, which, when combined with a typical co-linear/discone antenna gain of around 3Ã¢â‚¬â€œ5 dBi and modest feeder losses,
comfortably supports reception at line-of-sight ranges of several hundred kilometres for high-altitude aircraft.

The Mode-S Extended-Squitter downlink uses a binary modulation scheme called Pulse-Position Modulation (PPM). Each data bit occupies a fixed time slot of 1 microsecond, which is itself divided into two half-microsecond chips; a logical ONE is represented by RF energy present in the first half and absent in the second half of the slot, while a logical ZERO is represented by the opposite pattern Ã¢â‚¬â€ energy absent in the first half and present in the second. This scheme has the useful property that every bit period contains exactly one rising and one falling edge of RF energy, which simplifies clock recovery at the receiver and makes the signal robust against simple amplitude-only interference, since the decoder can examine the *relative* energy in the two half-bit intervals rather than relying on an absolute amplitude threshold [3].
Each Extended-Squitter transmission begins with a fixed, 8-microsecond preamble consisting of four short pulses (each 0.5 microseconds long) at precisely defined offsets

nominally at 0.0, 1.0, 3.5 and 4.5 microseconds from the start of the transmission followed by 7.5 microseconds with no pulses before the data block begins. This distinctive pulse pattern, illustrated in Figure 2.2, gives a receiver a highly reliable signature against which to correlate the incoming signal: a candidate preamble is declared only when pulses are observed at all four expected offsets and at no other intermediate offset, which provides good rejection of noise and of overlapping transmissions from other aircraft ("garbling"). Once a valid preamble has been detected, the receiver knows precisely where the 56-bit (short, DF11) or 112-bit (long, DF17/DF18) data block begins, and can proceed to demodulate it bit by bit using the PPM rule described above.

Downlink Format 17 (DF17) is the Extended-Squitter format used by Mode-S transponders to spontaneously broadcast ADS-B state-vector information; it is, in effect, the format that carries the bulk of the data of interest to this project. A DF17 frame is 112 bits (14 bytes) long and is organised into five principal fields, illustrated in Figure 2.1: a 5-bit Downlink Format field (DF, always equal to binary 10001 = 17 for Extended Squitter), a 3-bit Capability field (CA, indicating the transponder's level of Mode-S capability and current status), a 24-bit ICAO Aircraft Address field (AA, the unique identifier permanently assigned to that specific airframe), a 56-bit Message field (ME, whose internal structure depends on the message *type code* carried in its first five bits and which carries the actual payload Ã¢â‚¬â€ position, velocity, identification, etc.), and a final 24-bit Parity/Interrogator-Identity field (PI) [3], [6].
Fig. 2.2: Bit-level structure of a 112-bit Mode-S DF17 Extended-Squitter frame, showing the DF, CA, AA, ME and PI fields and their bit widths.

Unlike many communication protocols, Mode-S uses its 24-bit Parity/Interrogator-Identity field for integrity checking rather than appending a separate CRC trailer. Recomputing the polynomial remainder is a standard way to validate a raw Mode-S frame and remains important background theory for understanding the receiver. In the implemented architecture, however, RF demodulation, Mode-S framing and the associated low-level integrity handling occur inside the PingStation firmware. The Python application receives the PingStation's higher-level structured stream and therefore concentrates on TCP frame completeness, supported message layouts, field bounds, state continuity and timestamp validity.

The internal structure of the 56-bit ME field depends on a 5-bit Type Code (TC) sub-field at its head: type codes 1Ã¢â‚¬â€œ4 indicate Aircraft Identification and Category messages (carrying the flight's callsign, encoded six bits per character in a restricted alphabet); type codes 9Ã¢â‚¬â€œ18 and 20Ã¢â‚¬â€œ22 indicate Airborne Position messages (carrying CPR-encoded latitude/longitude and altitude); type code 19 indicates an Airborne Velocity message (carrying ground speed, track angle/heading and vertical rate); and several other type-code ranges are reserved for surface-position, status and operational messages that, while decoded where encountered, are of secondary importance to this project's objectives. The decoder implemented for this project (see Section 3.4.2) dispatches on this type-code sub-field to select the appropriate field-extraction logic for each message.

A subtlety that any ADS-B decoder must address is that the 56-bit ME field is too small to carry an aircraft's full latitude and longitude at the resolution required (better than five metres). The Extended-Squitter specification therefore uses a scheme called Compact Position Reporting (CPR), which divides the surface of the Earth into a regular grid and encodes only the aircraft's position *within* the current grid cell, using 17 bits each for latitude and longitude. Because this encoding is ambiguous on its own the same encoded value could correspond to many different grid cells each position message additionally carries a single "odd/even" format bit, and transponders alternate between odd-format and even-format encodings on successive transmissions. A receiver that has captured one message of each type within a sufficiently short time window (so that the aircraft has not moved between the two grid resolutions) can combine the two encodings to resolve the ambiguity and recover an unambiguous *global* position; alternatively, if the receiver already has a recent, trusted reference position for the aircraft (for example, from a previous globally-decoded fix), it can use a computationally simpler *locally* unambiguous decoding of a single message [3]. The decoding pipeline implemented for this project uses the globally-unambiguous, odd/even paired-message technique as its primary method, with

locally-unambiguous decoding relative to the aircraft's last known position used as a fallback when a matching paired message has not yet been observed mirroring the approach documented for reference decoders such as pyModeS [14].

Because aircraft may appear at any azimuth and at elevation angles ranging from just above the horizon (for distant, high-altitude traffic) to nearly overhead (for aircraft passing close to the receiving site), the receiving antenna must provide a radiation pattern that is omnidirectional in azimuth and reasonably uniform over a wide range of elevation angles. Two antenna types are commonly used for this purpose: co-linear (collinear) dipole-array antennas, which stack several half-wave radiating elements in phase to achieve increased gain in the horizontal plane at the expense of vertical beamwidth, and discone antennas, which provide very wide bandwidth and a smoothly omnidirectional pattern with moderate gain. Figure 3.8 shows an idealised polar plot of the azimuthal radiation pattern expected of such an antenna: essentially circular (omnidirectional) in azimuth, which ensures that aircraft are received with comparable signal strength regardless of their bearing from the ground station.
Fig. 3.1: Idealised azimuthal (polar) radiation pattern of a co-linear / discone 1090 MHz receiving antenna, showing the near-omnidirectional coverage required for ADS-B ground-station reception.

The antenna's gain, polarisation (vertical, to match the vertically polarised transmissions from aircraft transponders), voltage standing-wave ratio (VSWR) at 1090 MHz, and mounting height above surrounding obstructions all directly affect the achievable signal-to-noise ratio and hence the reception range and decoding success rate discussed quantitatively in Chapter 4. For the laboratory installation used in this project, the antenna was mounted as high as practicable on the building roof, with a short, low-loss coaxial feeder run to the PingStation receiver, in order to maximise the received signal level and minimise additional noise injected by the feeder system.

The uAvionix PingStation performs RF reception and low-level demodulation in its firmware and connects to the application over TCP. The application listens on a configurable local port (30003 by default) and receives a continuous binary byte stream. TCP does not preserve application-message boundaries, so a single network read may contain part of one frame, several complete frames, or a mixture of both. The software therefore retains incomplete bytes and uses the PingStation frame-length field to reconstruct complete messages before decoding. Simulation mode replays captured hexadecimal payload lines through this identical frame-splitting and decoding path.

For every application session, the capture logger creates separate HEX and ASCII text files, an exact unfiltered STREAM.bin file, and a RAW.txt JSON-lines file containing decoded records before preprocessing. The session also contains an icao_excel directory and a master workbook. This staged logging distinguishes the original receiver bytes, printable callsign evidence, intermediate decoder output and final normalised flight records, making faults traceable without mixing different processing levels.

The decoding stage first separates the continuous byte stream into complete length-prefixed frames. Obvious noise lengths are skipped and an incomplete trailing frame is retained until more bytes arrive. Each complete frame is then interpreted using the observed PingStation compressed-message layout and legacy fallbacks. The decoder extracts the ICAO address, callsign, latitude, longitude, altitude, ground speed, heading, vertical speed and squawk when those fields are present. Latitude/longitude candidates are checked against valid geographic ranges, and when more than one byte layout appears numerically valid, continuity with the aircraft's previous position is used to select the plausible result.

Decoding is incremental because individual PingStation frames may contain only a subset of the complete aircraft state. A dictionary keyed primarily by ICAO address preserves the latest known values and merges only fields present in each new frame. Zero-valued updates are prevented from erasing valid speed, heading or vertical-rate information unless they are meaningful. Each record also carries its timestamp, source address, frame length and an internal last-seen time, allowing stale aircraft to be removed from the active snapshot while retaining their stored history.

The preprocessor converts the decoder's flexible records into a stable application schema. Latitude and longitude are represented as decimal degrees; altitude is normalised to millimetres internally; heading is stored as degrees multiplied by 100; horizontal and vertical velocities are stored in centimetres per second; callsign and ICAO identifiers are upper-cased; and timestamps are normalised to ISO format. Record-level validation is performed through frame completeness, field presence, numeric conversion, geographic bounds and continuity checks. Low-level RF demodulation and Mode-S integrity handling are responsibilities of the PingStation firmware rather than being recomputed by the current Python preprocessor.

The prediction subsystem is designed to bridge a short interruption in ADS-B reception, not to generate a complete strategic flight plan. An aircraft is eligible for prediction only after it has previously supplied genuine observations during the current session and its ICAO address is no longer present in the active receiver snapshot. The predictor therefore never replaces valid live data. When reception resumes, the newly received state immediately becomes authoritative and the predicted display record is removed. The prediction horizon is limited by FLIGHT_PREDICTION_MAX_AGE_SEC, which is 180 seconds by default, because uncertainty grows rapidly when an aircraft turns, changes speed, climbs or descends.

For each temporarily missing aircraft, FlightTrajectoryStore retrieves up to the twenty most recent genuine trajectory samples. At least four valid timestamped samples are required. The timestamps are converted to elapsed time values, and three independent straight-line models are fitted: latitude as a function of time, longitude as a function of time and altitude as a function of time. Fitting a fresh local model for each aircraft and each outage makes the method an online statistical-learning baseline rather than a globally trained neural model.

In these equations, t_i is the elapsed time of observation i, y_i is the latitude, longitude or altitude value, b is the least-squares slope and a is the intercept. The future latitude, longitude and altitude are evaluated at the current prediction time. The fitted latitude and longitude slopes are converted to horizontal velocity and bearing, while the altitude slope provides vertical velocity. Geographic bounds and finite-number checks are applied before a predicted state is returned.
3.6.3 Why the Regression Is More Stable Than Two-Point Extrapolation

A two-point method calculates motion from only the final pair of observations. Any coordinate quantisation, timestamp jitter or single erroneous measurement directly changes its estimated speed and direction. Ordinary least squares instead chooses the line that minimises the sum of squared residuals across several recent observations. Positive and negative measurement errors tend to offset one another, and one noisy point has only partial influence on the fitted slope. The sliding window also prevents very old flight phases from dominating the current estimate. Consequently, the displayed continuation is usually smoother and less sensitive to one abnormal ADS-B update, while still adapting as new samples enter the window.

If fewer than four suitable samples are available, the timestamps have no usable spread or the regression produces a non-finite result, the system falls back to constant-velocity kinematics. Missing motion values are estimated from the latest two stored positions where possible. Distance is calculated as speed multiplied by outage duration, latitude and longitude are projected along the latest heading, and altitude is updated from the vertical rate. Every generated record is marked isPredicted and includes predictionAgeSec and the source label PREDICTED. The interface draws its continuation as a red dotted line. Predicted rows are deliberately excluded from trajectory_samples and the Excel training records so that later models are trained only on genuine receiver observations.

3.6.6 Justification for Selecting Sliding-Window Linear Regression

Sliding-window OLS regression was selected as the primary method because it provides the best balance for the current implementation rather than because it is universally the most accurate trajectory algorithm. It works immediately with each aircraft without a pre-collected labelled dataset, executes in negligible time for a twenty-sample window, has very small memory requirements, and exposes coefficients whose physical meaning can be explained and audited. Compared with constant-velocity extrapolation, it uses several observations and therefore suppresses isolated noise. Compared with Kalman-family filters, it avoids covariance-model selection and tuning at this stage. Compared with tree ensembles, LSTM/GRU networks and Transformers, it does not require extensive historical trajectories, route labels, weather inputs or offline training hardware.

The choice is therefore scientifically appropriate for short reception gaps in a single-station educational tracker. It also establishes a reproducible baseline against which more advanced models can be measured. A future research study should compare constant velocity, OLS regression, Kalman filtering and at least one trained sequence model on held-out trajectories using Haversine position error, altitude mean absolute error, heading error, root-mean-square error, inference latency and memory consumption. Results should be reported separately for straight cruise, turns, climbs, descents and different prediction horizons.

Taken together, the tests show that the current application performs the complete operational pipeline required for the project: it accepts live or replayed PingStation data, reconstructs complete frames, decodes and normalises dynamic aircraft records, logs each session at multiple processing stages, maintains compact historical trajectories, bridges short reception gaps with clearly labelled predictions, and updates an interactive map at approximately one-second intervals. The results also identify clear research limits: the receiver is single-station, online route/type enrichment is best-effort, polling contributes visible latency, and the baseline predictor cannot anticipate future turns or flight-plan constraints.
SUMMARY, CONCLUSION AND SCOPE FOR FUTURE WORK

This project designed and implemented an end-to-end ADS-B aircraft-tracking platform spanning 1090 MHz reception theory, PingStation TCP acquisition, length-prefixed frame separation, proprietary-message decoding, incremental state merging, unit normalisation, SQLite time-series storage, session-based HEX/ASCII/RAW capture, automatic per-ICAO Excel and master-workbook generation, short-outage trajectory prediction, optional aircraft/route enrichment, and a Leaflet.js/Chart.js/Flask dashboard. The final interface includes smooth marker movement, actual and red dotted predicted paths, route and aircraft tabs, status feedback, a direct simulation switch, a resizable information panel and graceful continuation of the core tracking functions when internet services are unavailable.

Every objective set out in Section 1.3 was therefore addressed: the relevant RF theory was studied and documented; the front-end was set up and characterised; the decoding, storage, prediction and visualisation pipeline was designed, implemented and integrated into a single, coherent application; and the resulting system was

evaluated quantitatively and discussed in relation to the wider field. The deliverable is a complete, self-contained, documented and (via PyInstaller) packaged application that can be operated, demonstrated and extended well beyond the duration of the academic project itself.

Several conclusions can be drawn. First, a PingStation and a single-host Python application can provide a practical local aircraft-tracking and logging platform without dependence on a commercial aggregation network. Second, using the same decoder for live and replay data makes captured sessions valuable for repeatable debugging and regression testing. Third, a sliding-window linear-regression model provides an interpretable, computationally inexpensive baseline for bridging brief reception gaps and is more resistant to isolated noisy samples than two-point extrapolation, although it cannot anticipate manoeuvres. Finally, the separation of acquisition, decoding, preprocessing, storage, prediction and presentation made substantial iterative corrections possible without destabilising the rest of the system.

The implementation has important limitations. It relies on one receiver and cannot independently validate an aircraft position through multilateration. The decoder is based on observed PingStation message layouts and should be validated against additional firmware versions and captures. SQLite stores coordinates to six decimal places, while eight-decimal formatting in Excel does not create accuracy beyond that present in the received data. The regression predictor assumes that the recent trend continues and is therefore intended only for short outages; it has no knowledge of airways, weather, air-traffic-control instructions or filed flight plans. Scheduled routes, aircraft metadata, photographs and base-map tiles depend on external services, although their failure does not stop local reception, decoding, logging or marker updates. The client still uses periodic polling and the application is designed for a single-host laboratory deployment.
Building on the foundation established by this project, several directions for future enhancement can be identified, broadly in increasing order of implementation effort:

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ Multilateration-based position validation: by deploying additional, geographically distributed receiving stations and comparing the times of arrival of the same broadcast at each station, an independent estimate of an aircraft's position could be computed and cross-checked against its self-reported position Ã¢â‚¬â€ substantially increasing the trustworthiness of the displayed data and enabling detection of spoofed or malfunctioning transponders.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ Push-based update delivery: replacing the current 1 Hz polling mechanism with a push-based protocol such as WebSockets or Server-Sent Events would eliminate the dominant contribution to end-to-end latency identified in Section 4.5, providing a noticeably more immediate "live" experience without requiring any change to the underlying decoding or storage pipeline.

â€¢ Advanced trajectory-model comparison: evaluate the current linear-regression baseline against constant velocity, Kalman and Extended Kalman filters, gradient-boosted models, and LSTM/GRU sequence networks using held-out trajectories and clearly defined position, altitude and runtime metrics.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ Integration of additional surveillance sources: extending the data-source abstraction (Section 3.3.1) to ingest other surveillance feeds Ã¢â‚¬â€ for example, ASTERIX-encoded radar data, or the 978 MHz UAT link discussed in Section 2.2 Ã¢â‚¬â€ would broaden the system's coverage and enable interesting comparative studies between cooperative (ADS-B) and non-cooperative (radar) surveillance data for the same airspace volume.

â€¢ Data-quality and decoder validation: collect labelled captures from additional PingStation sessions and firmware versions, quantify field-decoding accuracy, and introduce automated replay tests for known ICAO, callsign, position and motion values.

Ã¢â‚¬Â¢ Deployment as a continuously running, multi-user service: extending the current single-host design to support concurrent access by multiple users Ã¢â‚¬â€ potentially including authentication, rate-limiting and horizontal scaling Ã¢â‚¬â€ would move the system closer to a production-grade deployment suitable for, for example, departmental or institutional use as a standing demonstration and teaching resource.

In closing, this project has demonstrated that a complete, useful and pedagogically rich aircraft-surveillance system can be built, on a modest budget and within an undergraduate timeframe, by combining a sound understanding of electronics-and-communication fundamentals with careful software engineering.
